title: 2020: A Year in Review

jokes.text: You'll burn the place to the ground.
jokes.setup: Charlie pitches fireworks inside the bar as a great idea.
jokes.punchline: Dennis delivers the obvious truth flatly, as if it's a minor inconvenience rather than a catastrophic objection.
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — four words dismissing a catastrophic idea as a mild concern. Dennis as straight man here is effective, though not especially inventive.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: What if we let off some fireworks in here, huh? Fireworks in the bar? It's never been done before. Right?

jokes.text: Or a woman who was assigned male gender at birth but has retained her traditional love of the game? Which she has the right to do. That is her right... Of course, it's 2021...
jokes.setup: The gang is riffing on all possible gender/interest permutations of the investor, trying to appear progressive.
jokes.punchline: The escalation lands on a trans woman who loves football — delivered with ceremonial solemnity as if this is the most enlightened position, while remaining entirely about stereotypes.
jokes.explanation: The joke skewers performative allyship — the gang solemnly affirms a trans woman's right to love football while still reducing her to a stereotype. The chorus of 'Of course,' 'That's fine,' 'That is her right' is perfectly calibrated cringe.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: If it's a guy, I got a football ready for him... What if it's a guy who hates football but loves flowers? Or a woman who loves football but hates flowers?

jokes.text: Hi. Sorry to interrupt. My name's Gary. I'm here to speak to the owners of Paddy's Pub. / Oh. Thank sweet Jesus. / All right! Gary. / This is a relief. / This I can wrap my head around.
jokes.setup: The gang has spent two minutes preparing for every possible gender/identity permutation of the investor.
jokes.punchline: Gary is the most stereotypically vanilla white guy imaginable. The gang's visible relief and 'thank sweet Jesus' demolishes all their performed progressivism instantly.
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the cold open and one of the episode's strongest. The structure is immaculate: two minutes of increasingly elaborate inclusivity performance, all collapsed by 'Thank sweet Jesus' the moment a standard white guy named Gary walks in. 'This I can wrap my head around' is the devastating character-specific kicker. Perfectly earned, perfectly timed, perfectly hypocritical — this is exactly the kind of joke Always Sunny does better than anyone.

dialogue.line: Or a woman who was assigned male gender at birth but has retained her traditional love of the game? Yes. Which she has the right to do. That is her right... Of course, it's 2021... That's fine.

jokes.text: Now that we all know that we see eye to eye, let's talk about you giving us that PPP loan.
jokes.setup: Gary has just been warmly received. Dennis assumes the shared identity means Gary is there to give them money.
jokes.punchline: Dennis conflates 'being the same kind of person' with 'being here to hand out loans,' revealing the gang's assumption that fellow white guys are automatically on their team.
jokes.explanation: Good beat that extends the hypocrisy joke from #5 — the gang's 'we see eye to eye' means 'you're like us so you'll help us.' Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Here's the bottom line, you guys: it's 2021, all bets are off, okay? The chances of this person walking in and being your typical vanilla white guy are slim to none.

dialogue.speaker: Gary
dialogue.line: Hi. Sorry to interrupt. Uh, my name's Gary.

jokes.text: When the world says slow, we say go. Or strike. Or attack.
jokes.setup: The gang is explaining their pandemic business philosophy to Gary.
jokes.punchline: What starts as motivational-poster language escalates immediately to 'strike' and 'attack' — revealing the gang's default setting is aggression.
jokes.explanation: Tight three-word escalation that tells you everything about the gang. 'Go' is motivational, 'strike' is alarming, 'attack' is completely unhinged. The speed of the escalation is what makes it work.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Oh, thank sweet Jesus. All right! Gary. This is a relief. It is so good to see you. This I can wrap my head around.

jokes.text: As an out-of-work bouncer, I was looking to pursue my other interests that would be as intellectually stimulating as choking out a jabroni and leaving him out in the street. Like my longtime dream of becoming an international country teen pop sensation.
jokes.setup: Mac describes his pandemic pivot to something 'intellectually stimulating.'
jokes.punchline: The pivot from 'choking out a jabroni' (presented as intellectually stimulating) to 'international country teen pop sensation' as equivalent or superior is completely unhinged and totally character-consistent.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. The specificity of 'international country teen pop sensation' is perfectly absurd, and framing bouncer violence as 'intellectually stimulating' at the same level is a great double joke. 'Jabroni' is the right word. The word 'longtime' applied to this dream is devastating. This is Mac-specific in the best way — his delusion is grandiose and completely genre-confused.

dialogue.speaker: Gary
dialogue.line: Oh, I'm so sorry. Uh, there must be some confusion. I'm not here to hand out PPP loans. I'm here to collect on ones you already have.

jokes.text: ♪ Girl, you give me feels when I see them heels / Let's ride on a horse, making love out in the fields / Out in the fields / Let me be your guy / Never mind them flies ♪
jokes.setup: Mac is performing his country teen pop song to Dennis.
jokes.punchline: The lyrics are aggressively bad — a strange mix of teen romance, agricultural imagery, and 'never mind them flies' as a sincere romantic reassurance.
jokes.explanation: 'Never mind them flies' is the standout — a genuinely funny bad lyric because it's specific, the logic is sound (horses have flies), but it completely kills the romance. The song commits to its own badness in an endearing way.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Hey, when the world says slow, we say go. That's right. Or strike. Or attack.

jokes.text: It feels like I'm asking her to forget the flies that are surrounding me, not the horse.
jokes.setup: Dennis is critiquing Mac's lyric 'Never mind them flies.'
jokes.punchline: Dennis's specific, logical parsing of why 'never mind them flies' implies the singer is personally fly-covered — delivered as a genuine lyrical note — is funnier than the original lyric.
jokes.explanation: The joke is that Dennis is treating this terrible song with the analytical rigor of a real producer. His specific reinterpretation of the lyric — that Mac might have a personal fly problem — is the kind of absurd-logical comedy the show excels at.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: As an out-of-work bouncer, I was looking to pursue my other interests that would be as intellectually stimulating as choking out a jabroni and leaving him out in the street. Like my longtime dream of becoming an international country teen pop sensation.

jokes.text: ♪ Never mind them thighs. ♪ / Thighs? Where-- What? Why thighs? / Yeah, well, maybe he's got thick, grotesque thighs and he's embarrassed about 'em.
jokes.setup: Dennis objects to 'never mind them flies,' so Mac improvises a replacement.
jokes.punchline: The replacement lyric 'never mind them thighs' is inexplicably worse. Charlie's explanation — maybe he has 'thick, grotesque thighs' and is embarrassed — treats it as a reasonable storytelling choice.
jokes.explanation: Charlie's earnest advocacy for the 'thick, grotesque thighs' interpretation is the joke — he's genuinely trying to help by finding a narrative justification for a nonsensical lyric. 'Grotesque' is the perfect word choice.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: ♪ Girl, you give me feels when I see them heels / Let's ride on a horse, making love out in the fields / Never mind them flies ♪

jokes.text: I can't stop thinking about the election. / The integrity of the election, right? Our democracy is at stake. / We were concerned that our guy wasn't gonna get a fair shot.
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis claim they can't focus on music because they're consumed with concern for democratic integrity.
jokes.punchline: The grandiose language ('integrity,' 'democracy at stake') is being used to describe their partisan anxiety about a specific candidate — set up to misdirect toward Trump.
jokes.explanation: This is the first plant for the Kanye misdirection — it works better on rewatch knowing the punchline. The language is hilariously overblown for what turns out to be fandom for a presidential longshot.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: It feels like I'm asking her to forget the flies that are surrounding me, not the horse.

jokes.text: Mac and Dennis abandon the song entirely because they 'can't stop thinking about the election' — framed as an interruption to serious musical work
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are supposedly in a serious creative session on their musical project (a PPP loan business)
jokes.punchline: Their inability to focus is treated with the same gravity as a serious artist distracted by world events — except the 'art' is a terrible country teen pop song about horse flies
jokes.explanation: Transitional joke that moves the story forward. The irony of treating a terrible song session as serious creative work interrupted by civic duty is functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: ♪ Never mind them thighs ♪

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Thighs? Where What? Why thighs?

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, maybe he's got thick, grotesque thighs and he's embarrassed about 'em.

jokes.text: It's like, do I want a bunch of eggheads who spend all day learning about shit influencing how I think about things? No.
jokes.setup: Mac is explaining why the mainstream media dismissal of 'their guy' is unfair.
jokes.punchline: Mac describes expertise ('eggheads who spend all day learning about shit') as a disqualifying trait for influencing public opinion — delivered with complete sincerity.
jokes.explanation: 'Eggheads who spend all day learning about shit' as a dismissal of expertise is very quotable and perfectly Mac. The 'learning about shit' construction is funny because it's simultaneously accurate (they learn things) and contemptuous (but it's just shit).

dialogue.line: I can't stop thinking about the election... Our democracy is at stake... we were concerned that our guy wasn't gonna get a fair shot

jokes.text: You want a guy who knows how to party. And our guy knows how to party.
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are describing the qualities that make their candidate appealing.
jokes.punchline: In context — deliberately — sounds like Trump praise, but is actually about Kanye West, making 'knows how to party' land very differently on rewatch.
jokes.explanation: Part of the sustained Kanye misdirection. Gets stronger on rewatch when you know the punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Do I want a bunch of eggheads who spend all day learning about shit influencing how I think about things? No.

jokes.text: Oh. Look at this one, with the New York hat. She got bussed in from that liberal hellscape? All right, let's go find out. Let's talk to her. Excuse me, ma'am? Ma'am, yes. Hi. Ma'am. Are you registered to vote here? Are you from Philly?
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis, wearing tactical gear, are 'protecting' a polling place.
jokes.punchline: Their voter intimidation strategy — approaching a woman wearing a NY hat and demanding she prove she's local — is delivered with friendly customer-service energy while being obviously threatening and illegal.
jokes.explanation: The comedy of their voter intimidation being indistinguishable from aggressively friendly concern is classic Always Sunny. The repeated 'ma'am' is a good running beat.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Look at this one, with the New York hat. She got bussed in from that liberal hellscape?

jokes.text: We're gonna ask you a series of Philly-related questions in no particular order. Why do we hate Chris Chelios? Who is Uncle Eddie Savitz? Who is a better athlete, Donovan McNabb or Rocky Balboa?
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are testing a voter's Philly authenticity.
jokes.punchline: The 'Philly authenticity test' includes a fictional character (Rocky Balboa) presented as a real athlete, alongside a genuinely infamous local figure (Uncle Eddie Savitz, a notorious pedophile) as if these are equivalent cultural touchstones.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The specific Philly cultural knowledge makes it land harder for anyone who knows the references. Uncle Eddie Savitz being included as a straight 'you should know this' Philly question alongside Chris Chelios is dark and brilliant — only someone from Philly would include that name, and the show trusts the audience enough to leave it uncommented. Rocky Balboa as a sincere athlete comparison question is the perfect absurdist anchor.

dialogue.line: We're gonna ask you a series of Philly-related questions in no particular order... Who is Uncle Eddie Savitz? Who is a better athlete, Donovan McNabb or Rocky Balboa?

jokes.text: Sly Stallone is just a meatball actor. / Then why do we make statues to him?
jokes.setup: Dennis dismisses Stallone as 'just a meatball actor.'
jokes.punchline: Mac's rebuttal is the statue of Rocky in Philadelphia — which is real and has been a civic controversy — presented as proof of Stallone's athletic legitimacy.
jokes.explanation: 'Then why do we make statues to him?' is a perfect five-word demolition of Dennis's point — and it's not entirely wrong, which makes it funnier. 'Meatball actor' is also a great coinage.

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.line: Rocky Balboa is a fictional character, so this isn't even a conversation.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Are you saying you want Sly Stallone to be the starting QB for the Eagles next season?

jokes.text: So I'm sorry, now you're comparing McNabb to a teeny-tiny little man who's named after a woodwind instrument?
jokes.setup: Dennis introduces Doug Flutie as a comparison to Rocky.
jokes.punchline: Mac dismisses Flutie as 'named after a woodwind instrument' — 'flute' in 'Flutie' — delivered as if this is a devastating athletic disqualification.
jokes.explanation: The 'woodwind instrument' insult is a great comedy word — specific, unexpected, and genuinely funny as an athletic dismissal. The 'teeny-tiny little man' preface (Flutie was notably short) earns it further.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: So was Doug Flutie.

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.line: You saying he's an actor?

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: No, I'm say— He's one of the greatest football players that Canada ever produced.

jokes.text: Suffice to say, our arguing did not help the situation. / Yeah, it turns out they had their own security there to keep things safe, and they just kicked us right out.
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are recounting the polling place incident to Gary.
jokes.punchline: The understatement of 'our arguing did not help the situation' and the confused surprise that polling places have official security is a perfect double beat.
jokes.explanation: Functional recapping beat that wraps the polling place sequence. The understated delivery works but isn't particularly inventive.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Now you're comparing McNabb to a teeny-tiny little man who's, uh, named after a woodwind instrument?

jokes.text: Brian the security guard shows up and walks them back to the 100-foot limit, and Mac and Dennis immediately become deferential and offer to get him a coffee
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis have been aggressively intimidating voters
jokes.punchline: The moment any authority figure appears, they completely fold — offering coffee, calling him by name ('Good to see you again, Brian'), suggesting they'll 'be less effective back there' as though this is a legitimate professional concern
jokes.explanation: 'We'll be less effective back there' is the best line here — treating their voter intimidation like a job performance metric. The Gang's pattern of cowardice in the face of authority is well-established and this executes it cleanly.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Hey, what's up, Brian? Good to see you again... You want us back at the hundred feet? We'll go back to the hundred.

jokes.text: ♪ Freedom is the choice you have / Is it Rocky or McNabb? / Cast your vote and make it clear / Place your voting choice in here ♪
jokes.setup: Kicked out of the polling place, Mac and Dennis pivot to music as a way to influence the election.
jokes.punchline: The 'vote' song conflates the presidential election with the Rocky vs. McNabb debate — a ballot box for the sports argument becomes a de facto voting booth.
jokes.explanation: Brilliant payoff to the Rocky/McNabb argument — their solution to being removed from the polling place is to set up their own 'election' about the sports debate, complete with ballot boxes. The callback is structurally perfect: the digression becomes the pivot. 'Is it Rocky or McNabb?' in a song about voting freedom is an inspired absurdist collision.

dialogue.line: ♪ Freedom is the choice you have / Is it Rocky or McNabb? / Cast your vote and make it clear ♪

jokes.text: Now, the labeling... in hindsight, was a bit obtuse and created a great deal of confusion.
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis placed their ballot boxes 'all over the damn place' during the election.
jokes.punchline: Their pseudo-ballot boxes for a Rocky vs. McNabb poll are blamed — with complete sincerity and corporate PR language ('obtuse,' 'great deal of confusion') — for the national vote count delays.
jokes.explanation: The corporate euphemism ('obtuse,' 'kerfuffle') for accidentally interfering with a presidential election is the right register. The escalation from 'sports poll boxes' to 'caused national vote count delays' is well-paced.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: The labeling was a bit obtuse and created a great deal of confusion... we might have been entirely responsible for the vote delays

jokes.text: No, I'm saying we might have been entirely responsible for the vote delays.
jokes.setup: Gary asks if they're 'partially' responsible for the presidential vote count delays.
jokes.punchline: Mac corrects 'partially' to 'entirely' — delivered not as a confession but as a point of clarification and mild pride.
jokes.explanation: The correction from 'partially' to 'entirely' is a great beat — the precision of the self-incrimination, delivered not as shame but as accuracy, is very Always Sunny. Economy is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Gary
dialogue.line: What were you importing?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Inks, grease, paste. Sludges in general.

jokes.text: Why don't we play you a couple of our original songs, loosely based on the chord progressions of Emerson, Lake & Palmer?
jokes.setup: Gary is reeling from learning they caused the national vote delays.
jokes.punchline: Mac's response to this crisis is to offer to play their original songs — with the specific, pretentious detail that they're 'loosely based on Emerson, Lake & Palmer.' Nobody asked about music.
jokes.explanation: The 'loosely based on Emerson, Lake & Palmer' detail is the right level of pretentious specificity to make this funny — it's not a cool reference, it's the wrong reference, applied with total confidence.

dialogue.line: And, uh, what were you exporting?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Hair dye.

jokes.text: Inks, grease, paste. Sludges in general.
jokes.setup: Gary asks Frank what he was importing through 'Frank's Imports and Exports.'
jokes.punchline: Frank lists his imports with the casual authority of a legitimate businessman: 'inks, grease, paste. Sludges in general.' The category 'sludges in general' is the punchline — both specific and vague, clearly illegal-adjacent.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Frank line. 'Sludges in general' as a business category is an extraordinary bit of writing — it sounds just legitimate enough that he could be importing industrial supplies, while being exactly the kind of thing Frank would be trafficking. The escalation from 'inks' to 'sludges' is a beautiful three-step. Maximum economy (four words) for maximum Frank-ness. This is a textbook character comedy line.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: When society hits the brakes, I hit the gas, baby. Society break, I got gas.

jokes.text: When society hits the brakes, I hit the gas, baby. Society break, I got gas.
jokes.setup: Frank is explaining his pandemic philosophy of going harder when others slow down.
jokes.punchline: Frank's inspirational mantra 'Society hits the brakes, I hit the gas' degrades instantly to 'Society break, I got gas' — the word 'gas' shifting from metaphor to literal flatulence while Frank apparently doesn't notice.
jokes.explanation: Elegant double meaning — a motivational business philosophy becomes a fart joke in the span of four words. The degradation from 'gas (fuel)' to 'gas (flatulence)' is handled with perfect economy and Frank-specific dignity. The other character's immediate literal interpretation ('If you have gas, take it out in the hall') extends the joke well.

dialogue.line: If you have gas, take it out in the hall, okay?

jokes.text: What? If you have gas, take it out in the hall, okay? Also, I need another bucket. I'm out of paint here.
jokes.setup: Frank is delivering his 'I hit the gas' speech during what turns out to be an underground hair dyeing session.
jokes.punchline: Someone responds to Frank's metaphor as literal flatulence AND casually asks for more hair dye paint, revealing the chaotic context of the scene.
jokes.explanation: Good contextual reveal beat — we gradually understand that Frank is in some underground hair salon. The 'I need another bucket' line is a funny non-sequitur that starts to paint (literally) the scene.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: You look crazy, dude. Where you going?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I'm out.

jokes.text: Yeah, but you got to cover your nose, dude. You got to... / Why does nobody old know how to wear a mask?
jokes.setup: Frank is rushing out and someone tells him to wear a mask.
jokes.punchline: 'Why does nobody old know how to wear a mask?' is the universal pandemic frustration delivered as a character observation about Frank specifically.
jokes.explanation: Topical joke that lands because of its universality during 2020. Not the most original beat — this was a common complaint — but efficiently delivered.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Why does nobody old know how to wear a mask?

jokes.text: Fortunately, my favorite bookstore never closes, and they never judge their customers.
jokes.setup: Frank says he went to his 'favorite bookstore' to clear his head during the pandemic.
jokes.punchline: The store 'never closes' and 'never judges' — clearly an adult bookstore, delivered as if it's a charming independent shop. The mask exchange at the door confirms it.
jokes.explanation: Classic Frank misdirection — 'bookstore' that never closes and never judges is a beautifully understated euphemism. The deadpan delivery makes it land harder than a direct reference would. Very character-specific to Frank.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Fortunately, my favorite bookstore never closes, and they never judge their customers.

jokes.text: So I grabbed a few titles and I went in the back to do some light reading. There I was, staring at my idols, Peter North, T.T. Boy, the late, great D.P. Ram.
jokes.setup: Frank is describing his visit to the adult bookstore as if narrating a dignified memoir.
jokes.punchline: Frank's 'idols' are famous adult film performers, listed with reverence alongside the honorific 'the late, great' — treating pornography legends as cultural heroes deserving of the same respect as jazz musicians.
jokes.explanation: The 'late, great D.P. Ram' construction — using the funeral honorific for a pornography performer — is the kind of Frank-specific joke that only works because of DeVito's complete commitment. Peter North and T.T. Boy as 'idols' frames this as a moment of genuine inspiration. This is Frank at his most Frank.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: There I was, staring at my idols, Peter North, T.T. Boy, the late, great D.J. Ram.

jokes.text: And that's when I noticed it. The bad dye job. Who had I become? I was letting the pandemic get the best of me. It had taken my manhood.
jokes.setup: Frank is at the adult bookstore in a moment of personal crisis.
jokes.punchline: Frank's 'rock bottom' — the moment that caused genuine soul-searching and a vow to change — is seeing his own bad dye job reflected in the ambient lighting of a pornography shop. His 'manhood' being taken by the pandemic refers to his hair dye.
jokes.explanation: Frank's 'manhood' being his hair dye confidence — located and rediscovered in an adult bookstore — is simultaneously absurd and touching in that specific Frank way. The pretentious 'Who had I become?' introspection landing here is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Shoe polish, India ink, permanent marker. I tried 'em all. Until I finally hit pay dirt. Chinese motor oil.

jokes.text: Well, I went home and immediately did something about it. After I popped off.
jokes.setup: Frank has had his moment of inspiration at the adult bookstore.
jokes.punchline: 'After I popped off' — casually dropped after the inspirational pivot, treating masturbation as a minor logistical step in his self-improvement journey.
jokes.explanation: One of the best Frank lines in the episode. The economy is perfect — 'After I popped off' is four words dropped as a subordinate clause, as if completing his adult bookstore visit is just a reasonable precondition before getting to work. Frank's complete lack of embarrassment is the joke. The structure (inspirational beat → 'after I popped off' → back to business) is immaculate.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Little did I know, my work was about to be in the national spotlight, on the head of America's mayor, Rudolph William Giuliani.

jokes.text: Shoe polish, India ink, permanent marker. I tried 'em all. Until I finally hit pay dirt. Chinese motor oil.
jokes.setup: Frank is narrating his DIY hair dye research process like a scientist pursuing a breakthrough.
jokes.punchline: The triumphant discovery after a montage of failed experiments is 'Chinese motor oil' — delivered with the gravity of a Nobel Prize moment.
jokes.explanation: The structure mirrors genuine scientific breakthrough storytelling — escalating failed attempts, then the eureka moment. 'Chinese motor oil' as the triumphant answer, delivered with pride and the visual of Frank applying it, is a great beat. The escalation from ink to motor oil is perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Funny thing about the spotlight, though, sometimes it burns too bright. And that was the moment I knew it was coming to an end.

jokes.text: I became the most sought-after underground hair stylist for like-minded older men yearning for a sense of community during the pandemic.
jokes.setup: Frank opens an underground hair salon using Chinese motor oil as dye.
jokes.punchline: 'Like-minded older men yearning for a sense of community' is an almost poignant description of Frank's clientele — men who want their hair dyed to look younger, meeting in secret — until you remember it's motor oil being applied to their heads.
jokes.explanation: The gap between the almost-touching community framing and the gross reality (motor oil hair dye applied by Frank) is the joke. Solid but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Gary
dialogue.line: Wait, so you're saying that the hair dye that's dripping down your face is the same dye used by Rudolph Giuliani during the presidential election?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Yeah.

jokes.text: He said his boss was a very connected man who needed a situation fixed. And this poor bastard was in the eye of the shitstorm.
jokes.setup: Frank is building toward revealing his famous client using noir-style narration.
jokes.punchline: Frank is narrating a Giuliani client reveal using the language of organized crime ('connected man,' 'situation fixed,' 'in the eye of the shitstorm') — turning a campaign PR disaster into a mob story.
jokes.explanation: The genre mismatch — mob film language applied to a hair dye client — builds anticipation well. Gets stronger with the Giuliani reveal.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Charlie and I, we're the last tit on the hog before the asshole.

jokes.text: On the head of America's mayor, Rudolph William Giuliani. I was proud of how my work stood up in the spotlight.
jokes.setup: Frank has been building suspense about his famous client whose hair dye would be in the 'national spotlight.'
jokes.punchline: The reveal is Giuliani — specifically the infamous press conference where hair dye visibly ran down his face — and Frank's pride in his 'work standing up in the spotlight' is the punchline, since the dye spectacularly failed on live television.
jokes.explanation: The Giuliani dye reveal is the peak of Frank's section. The irony of 'I was proud of how my work stood up in the spotlight' — when his work memorably did not stand up and created one of the most viral political images of 2020 — lands perfectly. The structure of the buildup (mob language, 'national spotlight') makes the payoff hit harder. This is the best-structured joke in Frank's arc.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I am so sorry for my partner's blue language. It does not represent our business, and it's extremely off-putting.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: It was just a joke.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Just stop.

jokes.text: Funny thing about the spotlight, though, sometimes it burns too bright. And that was the moment I knew it was coming to an end.
jokes.setup: Frank describes Giuliani's hair dye melting on live TV.
jokes.punchline: Frank frames the visual disaster of Giuliani's runny dye as a profound, almost philosophical observation about the price of fame — 'sometimes it burns too bright' — while showing (or implying) the actual footage.
jokes.explanation: The 'spotlight burns too bright' metaphor is applied to literal hair dye melting under studio lights. Good sustained irony, slightly stretched.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: That's a mask. Yeah, of Ronald Reagan, but... Ronald Reagan? That's Dennis.

jokes.text: It was my own fault. I got sloppy. Started cutting corners, using American motor oil.
jokes.setup: Frank is explaining why the Giuliani dye job failed catastrophically on TV.
jokes.punchline: Frank's explanation for the failure is switching from Chinese motor oil to American motor oil — presented as a catastrophic quality compromise, as if the specific origin of motor oil is a known variable in hair dye quality.
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback to the Chinese motor oil breakthrough. The implication that Chinese vs. American motor oil is a meaningful quality distinction in hair dye is a brilliant specific detail. Frank's self-flagellation over 'cutting corners' by using domestic motor oil treats this as a genuine artisanal compromise. Concise, character-specific, and funny on its own as well as a callback.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: 'Fauch the Grouch.' Right? 'Mama needs wine.' Right? And this is funny 'cause women are alcoholics who hate their kids.

jokes.text: Wait, you're saying that the hair dye dripping down your face is the same dye used by Rudolph Giuliani during the presidential election? / Yeah.
jokes.setup: Gary realizes the full picture of what Frank has been describing.
jokes.punchline: Gary's incredulous clarifying question is met with Frank's flat 'Yeah' — delivered while presumably still having dye running down his own face in real time.
jokes.explanation: The 'Yeah' punctuation after Gary's dawning horror is a perfect button. The visual of Frank having the same dye dripping down his face during this conversation is the implicit joke that makes Gary's reaction read as horror rather than curiosity.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Halloween store owners, they're gonna be, like, some of the richest people in America, Dee.

jokes.text: Well, of course you're confused, Gary. That's 'cause you're not a moron.
jokes.setup: Gary expresses confusion about 'Garments and Varmints.' Dennis says the name isn't confusing.
jokes.punchline: Dee's explanation for Gary's confusion is that he's not a moron — implying that only morons would understand or accept the name.
jokes.explanation: One of the sharpest one-liners in the episode. The structure is perfect: explanation of confusion → 'because you're not a moron.' It's an insult to the other gang members wrapped in a compliment to Gary, and it's completely out of nowhere. Excellent economy and very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Get the pelts, you bitch!

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: What pelts?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: The pelts! The pelts, you bitch! You insufferable bitch.

jokes.text: We've been on top of each other for a long time. / Yeah, yeah. Charlie and I, we're the last tit on the hog before the asshole.
jokes.setup: Dee and Charlie are explaining their pandemic bubble situation.
jokes.punchline: Charlie's idiom for 'at the bottom of the pecking order' is 'the last tit on the hog before the asshole' — delivered as a casual expression he uses regularly.
jokes.explanation: Classic Charlie-ism — an idiom that sounds like it could be a real thing said by someone from his background, but is specific enough to be clearly his own invention. 'The last tit on the hog before the asshole' is an extraordinary phrase that earns near-perfect quotability. Completely Charlie-specific and deeply funny.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: The pandemic had kind of disrupted the bar's natural ecosystem. There was a real uptick in raccoons, which consider rat brains a delicacy.

jokes.text: I am so sorry for my partner's blue language. It does not represent our business, and it's extremely off-putting.
jokes.setup: Charlie says 'the last tit on the hog before the asshole' in front of a government auditor.
jokes.punchline: Dee immediately issues a formal apology as if she's the professional adult in the room — despite being equally complicit in all the schemes and equally terrible.
jokes.explanation: Dee's PR-speak apology for Charlie is a decent beat but fairly predictable in a show built on these characters performing professionalism.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.line: Gentlemen. You got the stuff?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Absolutely. Give me one minute.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Hey. Digging that face paint. Very festive. What are you gentlemen celebrating?

jokes.text: That's a mask. / Yeah, of Ronald Reagan, but... / Ronald Reagan? That's Dennis.
jokes.setup: Charlie holds up a mask he made for the pandemic mask business. Gary sees Ronald Reagan.
jokes.punchline: Dee immediately corrects that it's supposed to be Dennis — implying the mask looks so bad it's indistinguishable from Ronald Reagan, which is both an insult to Dennis's appearance and to Charlie's craftsmanship.
jokes.explanation: Classic three-line joke structure: setup (here's a mask), complication (wait, that's Ronald Reagan), reversal (no, it's Dennis). The implication that Dennis looks like Ronald Reagan, delivered completely casually, is a solid character-specific insult.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: You're telling me that you provided the iconic costumes at the Capitol riots?

dialogue.speaker: Gary
dialogue.line: Yeah.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Yep.

dialogue.speaker: Gary
dialogue.line: Can't say they weren't good costumes, Gary.

jokes.text: Their big pandemic business idea is revealed to be selling COVID masks — but they're novelty/funny masks, not medical ones. Specifically: a Dee mask labeled as 'Ronald Reagan'
jokes.setup: Charlie announces their pandemic business pivot — masks, obviously the most needed product — with great excitement
jokes.punchline: The masks are novelty/costume masks, not medical. Dee holds up a mask of her own face and Charlie says it's Ronald Reagan — implying Dee looks like Ronald Reagan
jokes.explanation: The pivot from 'we made COVID masks' to 'novelty masks' to 'this Dee mask is Ronald Reagan' is a sharp three-step joke. Implying Dee's face resembles Ronald Reagan is a good Dee-specific insult that she can't even argue with since she made the mask herself.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Fire.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Oh!

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Huh?

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Shit, I see it.

jokes.text: 'Fauch the Grouch.' Right? Fau-- That's a great name. Who is that?
jokes.setup: Charlie is showing off his novelty mask designs.
jokes.punchline: Gary's response to 'Fauch the Grouch' (a Fauci/Oscar the Grouch mashup) — 'that's a great name, who is that?' — is the joke. Gary finds the wordplay clever without recognizing who it refers to.
jokes.explanation: The pun is decent (Fauci + Grouch = 'Fauch the Grouch'), and Gary's clueless appreciation is an okay beat, but it's a fairly standard wordplay joke.

dialogue.speaker: Gary
dialogue.line: You people have shamelessly gamed the system out of massive amounts of taxpayer dollars for fictitious businesses that have gone bankrupt, and still you have the nerve to ask for more money?

jokes.text: 'Mama needs wine.' Right? And this is funny 'cause women are alcoholics who hate their kids.
jokes.setup: Charlie is explaining the humor behind his 'Mama needs wine' novelty mask.
jokes.punchline: Charlie's explanation of the joke — 'it's funny because women are alcoholics who hate their kids' — is a deadpan unpacking of the actual subtext of the 'wine mom' stereotype, delivered as if he's clarifying for a confused audience.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Charlie's explanation deconstructs the entire 'wine mom' commodity culture in one sentence by simply stating the actual premise out loud. The deadpan tone — explaining this as if it's helpful clarification — makes it devastating. Perfectly Charlie (he's not trying to be edgy, he's genuinely explaining), and it has genuine satirical bite.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Well, that's what makes America the greatest country in the world. When you're in need, the government comes in and bails you out. Nothing made me more money than businesses I sent into bankruptcy.

jokes.text: Think about it, man. Everyone's been stuck together at home, they're all worried and shit. They're gonna want to come together at the end of next year, so, like, Halloween store owners, they're gonna be some of the richest people in America, Dee.
jokes.setup: Charlie is making a business case for pivoting from medical masks to Halloween costumes.
jokes.punchline: Charlie's pandemic economic theory — that Halloween store owners will become 'some of the richest people in America' because people need to 'come together' — is delivered with the conviction of an investor presenting a thesis.
jokes.explanation: Charlie's confident incorrect business prediction — that Halloween store owners will be the financial winners of the pandemic — is funny because it's both completely wrong and also contains a grain of Charlie-logic that sort of makes sense if you're as stupid as he is.

dialogue.speaker: Gary
dialogue.line: 'Washington outsider, not taken seriously by the liberal media, successful businessman, unsuccessful in love, electrifying onstage.' Oh, yeah. That's our guy.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: That's Kanye. Kanye West.

jokes.text: Are you sick of being jerked around by the fat cats in the Halloween industry?
jokes.setup: Charlie is narrating an infomercial-style ad for Garments and Varmints.
jokes.punchline: Charlie's ad opens by identifying 'fat cats in the Halloween industry' as the oppressive force his customers are rebelling against — implying there is a powerful, corrupt Halloween industrial complex.
jokes.explanation: 'Fat cats in the Halloween industry' is the right level of populist grievance misdirected at an absurd target. Charlie's grievance-politics infomercial voice treating Spirit Halloween as an oppressive cartel is good character work.

dialogue.speaker: Gary
dialogue.line: I do not believe any of you. None of this happened. There is no way that you were all involved in every major event of the past year. Why? Because you're not Forrest Gump!

jokes.text: It makes less sense than it did in the beginning. / You're telling it wrong. / Gary gets it. / No, I don't get it.
jokes.setup: Dee and Charlie's explanation of Garments and Varmints has gotten more confusing.
jokes.punchline: Charlie insisting 'Gary gets it' while Gary immediately says 'No, I don't get it' is a clean running gag beat.
jokes.explanation: Running gag on Gary not understanding — works fine as a beat but isn't exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Stop the count! Stop the count!

jokes.text: Get more pelts. / What pelts? / The pelts! The pelts, you bitch! / What are we doing with animal pelts? / I can't sew without the pelts! / Get the pelts, you bitch!
jokes.setup: Charlie and Dee are rushing to fill a large costume order and running out of materials.
jokes.punchline: The reveal that Charlie's costume-making requires animal pelts (raccoon skins from the bar basement), delivered with escalating rage as if 'get the pelts' is an obvious instruction that Dee is stupidly failing to follow.
jokes.explanation: The escalating 'pelts' exchange works because it's gradually revealing that this is a raccoon-pelt costume operation while maintaining the rhythm of a normal work argument. Charlie calling Dee a 'bitch' in the cadence of a frustrated senior partner is the right comedic tone. 'You bitch' as punctuation (used twice) has good rhythm.

jokes.text: Now, normally, I don't call Dee a bitch. That's sort of Dennis's thing. / Dee's a goddamn bitch! / Yeah. Uh, but, you know, her vulgar language was rubbing off on me.
jokes.setup: Charlie apologizes to Gary for calling Dee a bitch, noting it's not his usual behavior.
jokes.punchline: Dennis immediately interjects 'Dee's a goddamn bitch!' — confirming that it IS his thing, completely unprompted, while Charlie diplomatically explains the situational language contamination.
jokes.explanation: Perfect character comedy. Charlie setting up 'that's sort of Dennis's thing' as a mild deflection, only for Dennis to immediately confirm it with vehemence mid-apology, is structurally immaculate. The timing of Dennis's interjection landing while Charlie is trying to be diplomatic is what makes this land. Character-specific to both Charlie (earnest apology) and Dennis (genuine enthusiasm for the insult).

jokes.text: The pelts that Charlie's referring to, they're from raccoons that he was tanning in the basement of this bar.
jokes.setup: Gary is trying to understand what pelts Charlie needed.
jokes.punchline: Dee's matter-of-fact explanation that Charlie has been tanning raccoon hides in the bar basement — delivered as clarifying information rather than an alarming confession — is the punchline.
jokes.explanation: The casualness of 'tanning raccoon hides in the bar basement' as a clarifying explanation is perfect deadpan. Dee saying this like she's answering a reasonable question is good character work.

jokes.text: The pandemic had kind of disrupted the bar's natural ecosystem. There was a real uptick in raccoons, which consider rat brains a delicacy, which of course you know, Gary, and now it's all starting to make sense.
jokes.setup: Charlie is explaining why there were raccoon pelts available.
jokes.punchline: 'Which of course you know, Gary' — Charlie assumes the government auditor is familiar with raccoon/rat-brain ecology as shared cultural knowledge — and 'now it's all starting to make sense' when absolutely none of it makes sense.
jokes.explanation: Charlie's assumption that raccoon/rat ecology is common knowledge ('which of course you know, Gary') is perfectly in character — his world is so specific he assumes everyone lives in it. 'Now it's all starting to make sense' as a callback to the name confusion, delivered while making zero sense, is a great structural beat. This is a quintessential Charlie speech.

jokes.text: The costume customers turn out to be the Capitol rioters — Charlie and Dee meet people in face paint 'celebrating' and hand over animal-skin costumes plus a horned Viking hat
jokes.setup: Charlie and Dee finally deliver their costume order to mysterious out-of-state customers who arrive in face paint
jokes.punchline: The customers are Capitol rioters on January 6th — the 'QAnon Shaman' costume (animal skins + horned hat) is what Charlie and Dee provide
jokes.explanation: Excellent dark comedy execution. The reveal that Charlie's raccoon-pelt costumes + a horned hat created the QAnon Shaman look is audacious and well-constructed. The Gang inadvertently costuming the Capitol riot — with Charlie complimenting the face paint as 'very festive' — perfectly uses their obliviousness as the engine of the joke. 'Now let's go save this country!' landing just before the January 6th reference is very sharp timing.

jokes.text: We're protesting the election. / Okay, well, I can get behind that, 'cause our guy did not get a fair shake. / The whole thing is a sham. / Our guy got screwed, man.
jokes.setup: Charlie and Dee are bonding with the costumed men over shared political grievances — still appearing to be Trump-related.
jokes.punchline: This is another layer of the Kanye misdirection — 'our guy got screwed' sounds like Trump support but will be revealed as Kanye fandom.
jokes.explanation: Extends the 'our guy' misdirection well and deepens the irony of the gang being at the Capitol riot by coincidence. Works better on rewatch.

jokes.text: I'm especially proud of the stitching on the animal skins. That was all Charlie. / You know what I'd like to do? I'd love to throw in this cool hat for free. I think it really completes the look.
jokes.setup: Dee and Charlie are delivering raccoon-pelt costumes to what are revealed to be Capitol rioters.
jokes.punchline: Charlie gifting the QAnon shaman's horned hat as a 'completes the look' accessory — framed as a customer service gesture — is the reveal that the gang inadvertently costume-designed the January 6th rioters.
jokes.explanation: The reveal that the gang provided the iconic QAnon shaman costume for January 6th is one of the episode's best moments. 'I'd love to throw in this cool hat for free, I think it really completes the look' — Charlie gifting what becomes the most photographed costume of a historic domestic event as a customer service upsell — is structurally brilliant. The payoff of the raccoon pelts/Halloween costume plot is perfectly calibrated. This earns a high score for the structural elegance of multiple threads (pelts, costumes, election, their guy) converging in one image.

jokes.text: They all seemed pretty amped up. But we were, too. I mean, people have been dragging our guy's name through the mud, saying he wasn't fit for office. / Calling him a narcissist, saying he was mentally ill, and that all the people who showed up for his events were idiots. / Yeah, but that's 'cause they've never seen the guy onstage. I mean, he's electrifying onstage.
jokes.setup: Charlie and Dee are explaining why they were emotionally invested in their candidate after providing costumes to the rioters.
jokes.punchline: All the descriptors ('narcissist,' 'mentally ill,' 'electrifying onstage') perfectly describe both Trump AND Kanye — the misdirection is in full force here. 'Electrifying onstage' applied to Kanye is literally true in a different way.
jokes.explanation: The best setup beat for the Kanye reveal. 'Electrifying onstage' works for both but means completely different things, and 'narcissist, mentally ill' applied to Kanye is simultaneously accurate and an unexpected register shift. Good misdirection craft.

jokes.text: You're telling me that you provided the iconic costumes at the Capitol riots? / Yeah. / Can't say they weren't good costumes, Gary. / They were great costumes.
jokes.setup: Gary realizes the full implication of the costume delivery story.
jokes.punchline: The gang's response to 'you provided the January 6th costumes' is to agree and defend the quality of their craftsmanship — not the politics, not the event, just the stitch work.
jokes.explanation: 'Can't say they weren't good costumes' in response to providing Capitol riot gear is a perfect deflection — the gang's only point of professional pride is the craftwork, completely dissociated from the event. Character-specific (they value the wrong things) and very well-timed.

jokes.text: Probably shouldn't have done that in the bar. / Oh, is that right? / Yeah, I'm sorry, guys. / I was trying to get a little fanfare for the loan. / It was pretty-- It was kind of cool.
jokes.setup: A firework has just gone off inside the bar, nearly hitting Gary.
jokes.punchline: Charlie's post-incident assessment is that 'probably shouldn't have done that' while Mac defends it as 'kind of cool' — the gang's risk assessment happening after the firework has already fired.
jokes.explanation: Good extension of the fireworks bit. 'It was kind of cool' as Mac's post-chaos assessment is character-consistent, though the moment is carried more by the callback than the new writing.

jokes.text: You people have shamelessly gamed the system out of massive amounts of taxpayer dollars for fictitious businesses that have gone bankrupt, and still you have the nerve to ask for more money? / Well, that's what makes America the greatest country in the world. When you're in need, the government comes in and bails you out.
jokes.setup: Gary delivers his verdict on the gang's fraudulent PPP loan use.
jokes.punchline: Dennis responds to 'you defrauded the government' with sincere American patriotism — 'that's what makes America great, the government bails you out' — treating bailout culture as proof of American exceptionalism.
jokes.explanation: Dennis reframing government fraud as patriotism ('that's what makes America great') is a sharp satirical beat. The logic is internally consistent in the worst possible way, which is what makes it work as character comedy with genuine satirical bite.

jokes.text: Nothing made me more money than businesses I sent into bankruptcy. / Yes-- Yeah, yeah. / That's the American way.
jokes.setup: The gang is defending their failed fraudulent businesses as American.
jokes.punchline: Frank's contribution — 'nothing made me more money than businesses I sent into bankruptcy' — is simultaneously a credible Frank Reynolds business philosophy and a dark commentary on how bankruptcy can be used as a wealth-extraction tool.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Frank line that works on two levels: as a character moment (Frank genuinely has done this) and as satire of a specific type of American capitalist. Very economy-efficient and character-specific. The delivery paired with 'that's the American way' gives it the right sardonic frame.

jokes.text: 'Washington outsider, not taken seriously by the liberal media, successful businessman, unsuccessful in love, electrifying onstage.' / Oh, yeah. / Yeah, yeah, that's our guy. / Absolutely. Yeah. / That's Kanye. Kanye West.
jokes.setup: Gary has been listening to all the descriptions of their candidate and makes the obvious inference.
jokes.punchline: Gary says 'That's Trump' — the gang is baffled. It's Kanye West. The reveal lands because every descriptor (narcissist, outsider, electrifying onstage, unsuccessful in love) applies to both men, but the gang meant Kanye.
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode and one of the best payoffs in Always Sunny's later seasons. The Kanye reveal works on every level: (1) it's genuinely surprising because the misdirection is perfectly constructed over 20 minutes, (2) the descriptors work for both candidates which is itself a sharp political observation, (3) the gang's confusion at being accused of supporting Trump — 'where'd you get that?' — is perfect character work, (4) the entire Jan 6 sequence is retroactively reframed as the gang costuming Capitol rioters while trying to help Kanye's campaign. The episode builds to this. The setup/payoff ratio over 20 minutes is exceptional TV writing. 'Have you seen him onstage?' as the defense is a perfect final note.

jokes.text: I do not believe any of you. None of this happened. There is no way that you were all involved in every major event of the past year. / Wh-Why? / Because you're not Forrest Gump!
jokes.setup: Gary has heard all three stories of the gang's involvement in the 2020 election, Giuliani's hair dye, and the Capitol riots.
jokes.punchline: Gary's 'you're not Forrest Gump!' — the explicit acknowledgment of the episode's structural device (a Zelig-like character present at every major historical event) — is a meta-aware puncture of the premise.
jokes.explanation: 'You're not Forrest Gump!' is a great button on the entire episode's premise — explicitly naming the structural joke that the gang has been present at every 2020 event. Gary as the audience surrogate saying what everyone is thinking is well-timed. The meta acknowledgment works because it's angry rather than winking.

jokes.text: Okay. / I don't... I don't like him. / I don't think he's gonna give us the loan. / I don't think we're gonna get the loan, either.
jokes.setup: Gary has just told them he's reporting them to the IRS and storms out.
jokes.punchline: Dennis's flat 'I don't like him' — processing Gary's audit verdict as a matter of personal preference rather than professional catastrophe — is a perfect character beat.
jokes.explanation: 'I don't like him' as a response to being referred to the IRS is perfect Dennis — reducing catastrophe to personal taste. The subsequent 'I don't think we're gonna get the loan' as an understatement is a solid button.

jokes.text: You know what we should do? Let's listen to some Kanye West. / That's what we should do. That's gonna bring the mood back up.
jokes.setup: The gang has just been told they're being reported to the IRS.
jokes.punchline: Their response to fiscal ruin is to put on Kanye — their guy — as a morale solution. This is a callback to the entire Kanye misdirect and a perfect character note.
jokes.explanation: Good final beat — listening to Kanye after the reveal lands as a satisfying closing character note. The choice of 'Gold Digger' (a song about women who exploit men for money, as the gang has just tried to exploit the government for money) is an ironic grace note.

jokes.text: Stop the count! Stop the count!
jokes.setup: The gang is dancing to 'Gold Digger' by Kanye after all their PPP loan schemes have been exposed.
jokes.punchline: Mac shouts 'Stop the count!' — the actual post-election chant by Trump supporters — during a Kanye song, in the wake of their revealed Kanye fandom. The chant is recontextualized as either sincere or ironic, and the ambiguity is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Perfect two-word button on the entire election plot. 'Stop the count' during a Kanye party celebrates the gang's peculiar position — they caused vote count delays accidentally for a Kanye campaign that never had a path to victory. The ambiguity (are they Trump people appropriating the chant? Kanye people? Neither?) is sharp.

jokes.text: During 'Gold Digger' playback, someone yells 'STOP THE COUNT! STOP THE COUNT!' mid-song
jokes.setup: The Gang is listening to Kanye's 'Gold Digger' together as a post-audit coping mechanism
jokes.punchline: 'Stop the count!' — the Trump election integrity chant — is shouted mid-Kanye song, bringing together the two threads of the episode's misdirection in a final joke that works as both a callback and a tag
jokes.explanation: A good tag that ties the two political threads together. 'Stop the count' during a Kanye song is funny because it conflates the two political figures the episode has been playing with. Good economy — one line, two callbacks.

tmdb_overview: The Gang looks back on 2020 to justify their numerous PPE loans. In doing so, it is revealed that they contributed to the chaos of the past political year way more than anyone could have imagined.
